title: Mediant insertion — and the honest boundary with the open problem
content: The header frames the file as the verified arithmetic of mediant insertion, the operation that refines F_n into F_{n+1} by inserting the mediant (a+c)/(b+d) between adjacent fractions a/b < c/d. It states explicitly that the open Erdős #1005 lower bound f(n) ≥ (1/12 − o(1))n on runs of similarly ordered fractions is NOT resolved here; the file supplies the gap-splitting calculus and the optimality of the mediant on which such constructions rest. The file is self-contained (it does not import the parent's axiom longestSimilarRun) and 0-axiom.
mathContext: Farey sequence $F_n$: reduced $a/b \in [0,1]$ with $b \le n$. Mediant of $a/b, c/d$ is $(a+c)/(b+d)$; for a unimodular pair $bc-ad=1$ it first enters at order $b+d$.

title: Unimodular pairs and their order
content: Unimodular a b c d := b·c = a·d + 1 is the algebraic signature of Farey adjacency. unimodular_lt shows it forces the value order a/b < c/d: cross-multiplying via div_lt_div_iff₀ reduces to a·d < c·b, immediate from b·c = a·d + 1. Every theorem in the file takes this predicate as hypothesis.
mathContext: $a/b < c/d$ unimodular $\iff bc - ad = 1$; this single equation determines both adjacency and order.

title: The gap formula c/d − a/b = 1/(bd)
content: gap_eq: a unimodular gap has size exactly 1/(bd). The proof clears denominators with div_sub_div and div_eq_div_iff, turning the claim into the polynomial identity (cb − ad)·(bd) = bd, closed by linear_combination (b*d) * hu against the unimodular relation hu : bc = ad + 1. This is the quantity that mediant insertion subdivides.

title: Each split half is again unimodular — the recursive engine
content: unimodular_left and unimodular_right show the mediant forms a unimodular pair with each endpoint: b(a+c) − a(b+d) = bc − ad = 1 and (b+d)c − (a+c)d = bc − ad = 1. Both are one-line linear_combination identities over ℤ. Consequence: the two sub-gaps of a split are themselves Farey-adjacent and can be split again — this is precisely the recursion that generates the Stern–Brocot tree and enumerates every reduced rational exactly once.
mathContext: $bc-ad=1 \Rightarrow b(a+c)-a(b+d)=1$ and $(b+d)c-(a+c)d=1$: mediant insertion preserves unimodularity.

title: Mediant insertion splits the gap exactly
content: The gap-splitting calculus. mediant_gap_left: (a+c)/(b+d) − a/b = 1/(b(b+d)). mediant_gap_right: c/d − (a+c)/(b+d) = 1/(d(b+d)). subgaps_sum: the two sub-gaps recombine to the original, 1/(b(b+d)) + 1/(d(b+d)) = 1/(bd), so insertion loses no measure. Each gap proof clears denominators and closes with linear_combination against bc = ad + 1; the sum is a telescoping linarith over the three gap equations.

title: Ratio d:b and strict refinement
content: subgap_ratio: the left sub-gap scaled by b equals the right sub-gap scaled by d (both equal 1/(b+d)), so the two pieces stand in ratio d:b — the endpoint with the smaller denominator inherits the larger share. mediant_gap_left_lt: each sub-gap 1/(b(b+d)) is strictly smaller than the whole 1/(bd), since b(b+d) > bd; mediant insertion genuinely refines the partition rather than merely re-labelling it.

title: The denominator identity — the algebraic kernel
content: denom_identity: over ℤ, q = b·(cq − pd) + d·(pb − aq) whenever bc − ad = 1. Expanding the right side gives bcq − bpd + dpb − daq = q(bc − ad) = q. A single linear_combination (-q) * h verifies it. This unconditional identity is the entire engine of the minimal-denominator theorem: it expresses the denominator q of ANY fraction as a positive-integer combination of b and d.
mathContext: $q\,(bc-ad) = b(cq-pd) + d(pb-aq)$; with $bc-ad=1$ the left side is just $q$.

title: The mediant has the smallest denominator in the gap
content: denom_ge_of_between (headline): any fraction p/q strictly between two unimodular neighbours has q ≥ b + d. Cross-multiplying the strict orders a/b < p/q and p/q < c/d gives the integer inequalities pb − aq ≥ 1 and cq − pd ≥ 1 (extracted by omega after exact_mod_cast). Feeding these into the denominator identity with le_mul_of_one_le_right yields q = b·(cq−pd) + d·(pb−aq) ≥ b + d. The mediant (a+c)/(b+d) attains this bound, so it is the smallest-denominator fraction in the open gap.

title: Equality is attained only by the mediant
content: eq_mediant_of_denom_eq: if a strictly-in-gap fraction p/q attains the minimum q = b + d, then p = a + c — it IS the mediant. Since q = b·(cq−pd) + d·(pb−aq) with both brackets ≥ 1, equality q = b + d forces each bracket to exactly 1 (a linarith squeeze, then mul_left_cancel₀). From pb − aq = 1, q = b + d and bc = ad + 1, a linear_combination gives p·b = (a+c)·b, and cancelling b yields p = a + c. mediant_is_min_denominator packages the in-gap claim with the bound: the mediant lies strictly inside and minimises the denominator.
mathContext: $q=b+d$ with $q=b(cq-pd)+d(pb-aq)$ and both brackets $\ge 1$ forces each $=1$; then $pb-aq=1$ pins $p=a+c$.

title: Strict denominator growth and the depth-two refinement
content: mediant_denom_gt_left/_right note the trivial b < b+d and d < b+d, then interior_denom_gt_max upgrades §4's bound to max b d < q for any interior fraction. denom_ge_left_subgap and denom_ge_right_subgap apply unimodular_left/unimodular_right recursively, giving the depth-two denominator floors b+(b+d) and (b+d)+d for the two sub-gaps. The headline denom_ge_of_between_ne_mediant then shows any fraction other than the mediant itself has denominator ≥ (b+d) + min(b,d): the mediant alone attains b+d, and the next admissible denominator jumps by at least min(b,d) — the seed of any depth/counting argument toward runs.

title: One-sided chains grow denominators exactly linearly — correcting a false heuristic
content: unimodular_iterate_left/_right show that inserting the mediant k times into only the left (resp. right) sub-gap keeps the pair unimodular, turning a/b < c/d into a/b < (k·a+c)/(k·b+d). denom_ge_iterate_left/_right lift the §4 bound to this iterated pair, and iterate_left_denom_linear pins the k-th one-sided mediant's denominator to exactly (k+1)·b + d — linear in the depth k. This corrects the tempting heuristic that the order-n cap forces only O(log n) refinement levels: the all-left chain from 0/1 < 1/1 is 0/1, 1/2, 1/3, …, 1/n, giving Θ(n) admissible levels, the worst-case opposite of the balanced chain in §7.
mathContext: $k\text{-fold left insertion: denominator} = (k+1)b + d$, linear in $k$.

title: Balanced (Fibonacci) insertion grows denominators exponentially
content: fib_cassini proves Cassini's identity F_{n+1}² − F_n·F_{n+2} = (−1)ⁿ by a one-step induction; unimodular_fib_even reads it at even index to certify that consecutive Fibonacci fractions F_{2k}/F_{2k+1} < F_{2k+1}/F_{2k+2} are genuine Farey-adjacent pairs. fib_two_step_double and fib_pow_lower give 2ʲ ≤ F_{2j+1}, and balanced_mediant_denom shows the balanced mediant's denominator is exactly the next Fibonacci number F_{2k+3}. denom_ge_balanced specialises §4's bound to this pair, and balanced_depth_log concludes: if F_{2j+1} ≤ n then 2ʲ ≤ n, so only O(log n) balanced (alternating) levels fit under the order cap — an exponential separation from §6's Θ(n) one-sided chain.

title: Mediant chains are similarly ordered — the bridge to f(n), honestly incomplete
content: SimOrd a b c d holds when (a−c) and (b−d) share a weak sign — definitionally the similarlyOrdered relation of the parent file — with simOrd_iff_prod giving the equivalent product form (a−c)(b−d) ≥ 0. simOrd_mediant_left/_right show the mediant is similarly ordered with each parent endpoint, and simOrd_iterate_left_chain/_right_chain promote this to the whole §6 one-sided chain being pairwise similarly ordered; simOrd_chain_admissible packages this with the order-n cap to produce Θ(n)-long similarly ordered families. The section is explicit about the gap it does NOT close: the chain 0/1, 1/2, 1/3, …, 1/n is similarly ordered but its terms are not consecutive in F_n, so this is not yet a run in the sense of the open problem.

title: The classical three-term Farey successor recurrence
content: Formalises the Hardy–Wright successor e/f of c/d given consecutive neighbours a/b < c/d, carried additively as e+a = k·c, f+b = k·d to avoid ℕ truncation. farey_succ_unimodular shows the successor is again a genuine Farey neighbour of c/d; farey_succ_lt places it strictly to the right; farey_three_term gives the symmetric law d·(a+e) = c·(b+f), the Farey form of b_{k-1}+b_{k+1}=k·b_k; farey_succ_denom_le_iff identifies k = ⌊(n+b)/d⌋ as the order-n admissibility threshold. The headline simOrd_succ_controlling reduces a genuine consecutive step to the sign of (a+c−k·c)(b+d−k·d), and simOrd_succ_k_eq_one shows the k=1 step is always similarly ordered — a first, partial answer that §10 will make unconditional.

title: Every Farey-adjacent pair is similarly ordered — runs never break at a single step
content: unimodular_excl_cross_left and unimodular_excl_cross_right rule out the two sign-inversion patterns a unimodular pair could have; together they force the headline unimodular_simOrd: every unimodular (Farey-adjacent) pair satisfies SimOrd, not merely the k=1 successor step of §9. farey_succ_simOrd upgrades this to any consecutive step of any quotient k, and succ_controlling_nonneg shows the §9 controlling product (a+c−k·c)(b+d−k·d) is unconditionally ≥ 0. This corrects the §9 preamble's suggestion that large k could break a run at a single step: it cannot — the entire 1/12–1/4 obstruction lives strictly among non-adjacent pairs, which §11 onward isolates.

title: The first non-adjacent obstruction — length-3 runs and the outer window
content: Since §10 frees every adjacent pair, the smallest place a run of three consecutive Farey neighbours a/b, c/d, e/f can break is the outer (non-adjacent) pair a/b, e/f. simOrd_outer_iff shows this pair is similarly ordered iff (2a−k·c)(2b−k·d) ≥ 0, where k is the §9 successor quotient. simOrd_triple_iff_outer reduces the whole length-3 run to just this outer condition, and simOrd_triple packages the equivalence as the headline: a length-3 run is similarly ordered exactly when this single inequality on k holds — the first explicit, metric criterion for a run to break, controlled by an interval of width 2/(c·d).

title: Length-4 runs — two quotients and the Stern–Brocot product k₁k₂−1
content: A length-4 block a/b, c/d, e/f, g/h uses two successor quotients k₁, k₂. simOrd_long_iff shows the genuinely new long-range pair a/b, g/h (spanning the whole block) is similarly ordered iff ((k₂+1)a − (k₁k₂−1)c)((k₂+1)b − (k₁k₂−1)d) ≥ 0 — the coefficient k₁k₂−1 being the Stern–Brocot product, the combined depth of both steps. The headline simOrd_quad assembles the full run criterion as the conjunction of the two §11 length-3 windows (one per consecutive triple) plus this new long window; the three adjacent pairs remain free by §10.

title: Length-5 runs — three quotients and the continuant K(k₁,k₂,k₃)
content: Extending to a length-5 block with three successor quotients k₁, k₂, k₃, simOrd_long3_iff expresses the endpoint pair a/b, i/j's similar ordering as (k₂k₃·a − K·c)(k₂k₃·b − K·d) ≥ 0 with K = k₁k₂k₃ − k₁ − k₃ — the continuant of the three quotients, continuing the ladder K() = 1, K(k) = k, K(k₁,k₂) = k₁k₂−1 from §11/§12. simOrd_quint assembles the headline: the full length-5 criterion is the conjunction of six non-adjacent windows (three length-3, two length-4, one new length-5), with the four adjacent pairs free by §10 — the pattern that §14 will collapse into a single statement for every run length.

title: The continuant — one run-length criterion valid for every length
content: Replaces the per-length lemmas of §11–13 by a single statement. Continuant (with the head recurrence K(k₁::k₂::ks) = k₁·K(k₂::ks) − K(ks)) and secondCont are defined; stepSeq iterates the §9 successor recurrence over a whole quotient list, and stepSeq_eq_continuant proves the closed form stepSeq a c ks = K(ks)·c − secondCont(ks)·a by induction. endpoint_window then factors the endpoint product for a run of arbitrary length, and simOrd_run_iff is the headline: the run's endpoints are similarly ordered iff ((1+secondCont ks)·a − K·c)((1+secondCont ks)·b − K·d) ≥ 0. The rungs continuant_nil/one/two/three and the subsumption lemmas endpoint_window_one/two/three verify this recovers §11/§12/§13 exactly at |ks| = 1, 2, 3.

title: Depth-m unimodularity of the iterated Farey walk
content: stepPair returns the final consecutive pair (t_{|ks|}, t_{|ks|+1}) of the §14 recurrence, with stepPair_snd confirming its second component is exactly stepSeq. The headline stepPair_cross proves the cross-determinant of the numerator and denominator walks is invariant under every step: n_m·d_{m+1} − n_{m+1}·d_m = a·d − b·c, since each step's matrix [[k,−1],[1,0]] has determinant 1. stepPair_cross_unimodular specialises this to a unimodular seed: the entire §14 quotient-list walk consists of genuinely consecutive Farey fractions at every depth, not merely similarly-ordered ones — the depth-uniform strengthening of §9's single-step consecutiveness.
mathContext: $n_m d_{m+1} - n_{m+1} d_m = ad - bc$, invariant under the recurrence $(a,c)\mapsto(c,kc-a)$.

title: The continuant matrix — Cassini and reversal symmetry
content: Introduces a bespoke 2×2 integer matrix type Mat2 and the step matrix stepMat k = [[k,−1],[1,0]] (determinant 1), whose ordered product contMat ks = M(k₁)⋯M(kₙ) has top-left and bottom-left entries exactly Continuant ks and secondCont ks (contMat_entries) — the matrix face of the §14 recurrence. Because det is multiplicative, det_contMat gives det P(ks) = 1 at every depth, yielding the Cassini identity continuant_cassini. The anti-automorphism phi(X) = J·Xᵀ·J (J = diag(1,−1)) fixes every step matrix while reversing products, so contMat_reverse gives P(ks.reverse) = phi(P ks), and reading off the top-left entry proves the reversal-symmetry headline continuant_reverse: K(ks.reverse) = K(ks). continuant_append is Euler's classical composition law for continuants, read off contMat's multiplicativity on list append.

title: Continuant positivity and linear growth in the large-quotient regime
content: On a quotient list with every entry ≥ 2, secondCont_lt_continuant proves the core invariant 0 ≤ secondCont ks < Continuant ks by induction on the pair map (s,K) ↦ (K, k·K−s). This immediately gives strict positivity (continuant_pos), strict monotonicity under prepending (continuant_strict_mono), and the linear growth bound continuant_ge_length: Continuant ks ≥ |ks|+1. The section is equally careful to record the boundary: continuant_ones_two and continuant_ones_three witness that the all-1 (balanced) continuant already vanishes at length 2 (K[1,1]=0) and goes negative at length 3 (K[1,1,1]=−1) — positivity is strictly a large-quotient phenomenon, not universal.

title: The bottom-right entry and the classical three-term Cassini identity
content: Closes the one entry §16 left opaque: contMat_d shows the bottom-right entry of P(k::ks) equals the old top-right entry, −secondCont(ks.reverse). contMat_cons_eq then identifies all four entries of the continuant matrix as signed continuants of sublists, and continuant_cassini_full restates the Cassini determinant with no residual matrix entry. Via the bookkeeping lemmas dropLast_reverse_eq, secondCont_eq_continuant_tail and secondCont_reverse_eq, this specialises to the textbook continuant_cassini_classical: for a length-≥2 list L, K(L.dropLast)·K(L.tail) − K(L)·K(L.tail.dropLast) = 1, the recognizable three-term Cassini identity relating consecutive continuants.

title: Coprimality of consecutive continuants — Farey fractions are automatically reduced
content: Reads the §16 Cassini determinant K(ks)·(P ks).d + secondCont(ks.reverse)·secondCont(ks) = 1 as a Bézout identity: continuant_isCoprime concludes IsCoprime (Continuant ks) (secondCont ks). Since secondCont(k::ks) = Continuant ks definitionally, continuant_tail_isCoprime specialises this to IsCoprime (Continuant (k::ks)) (Continuant ks) — consecutive continuants along any Stern–Brocot path share no common factor, so the mediants produced by iterated insertion are automatically in lowest terms. continuant_isCoprime_reverse records the symmetric coprimality with the reversed trailing continuant.

title: Sharpness of the linear growth bound — the all-2 minimum
content: continuant_secondCont_replicate_two computes, by induction, that the constant list [2,…,2] of length n has Continuant = n+1 and secondCont = n — the Pell ladder 1, 2, 3, 4, … in which each large-quotient step adds exactly 1. continuant_ge_length_sharp packages this as a witness that §17's linear bound Continuant ≥ |ks|+1 cannot be improved in the large-quotient regime. continuant_head_mono complements this: raising the leading quotient never decreases the continuant, so the all-2 list is the continuant-minimiser among lists sharing a fixed all-2 tail — pinning down which large-quotient runs are metrically cheapest.

title: The balanced extreme — the all-ones continuant is period-6 and bounded
content: Writing aₙ = K(1ⁿ), sₙ = secondCont(1ⁿ), continuant_replicate_one_succ specialises the §14 recurrence (every quotient = 1) to the coupled linear system aₙ₊₁ = aₙ − sₙ, sₙ₊₁ = aₙ. Its companion matrix is the order-6 rotation [[1,−1],[1,0]], so continuant_secondCont_replicate_one proves the pair is 6-periodic; continuant_replicate_one_mod reduces any n to n mod 6, and the headline continuant_replicate_one_bounded shows K(1ⁿ) ∈ {1, 0, −1} for every n — the all-1 continuant never grows, the sharp opposite of the all-2 ladder's linear growth (§20). continuant_replicate_one_abs_le_one packages the bound as |K(1ⁿ)| ≤ 1.

title: The boundary of the positive cone — exactly one leading 1 is tolerated
content: On a large-quotient tail ks, continuant_one_cons gives the closed form K(1::ks) = K(ks) − secondCont(ks), and continuant_one_one_cons gives K(1::1::ks) = −secondCont(ks). Combined with §17's strict domination secondCont(ks) < K(ks), continuant_one_cons_pos shows one leading 1 keeps the continuant strictly positive, while continuant_one_one_cons_nonpos and continuant_one_one_cons_neg show a second consecutive 1 destroys positivity (strictly, once the tail is nonempty). So exactly one leading quotient may drop to 1 before crossing from §17's positive cone into the §21 period-6 orbit — the sharp crossing point between the two regimes.

title: Leading 1s on an arbitrary tail — the period-6 rotation in full
content: Generalises §21/§22 from the pure all-1 list to an arbitrary tail ks: continuant_three_ones_cons, continuant_four_ones_cons, continuant_five_ones_cons give the closed forms for 3, 4, 5 leading 1s, and continuant_secondCont_replicate_one_append proves the pair (K(1ʲ++ks), secondCont(1ʲ++ks)) is 6-periodic in j for every ks. The headline continuant_replicate_one_append_orbit gives the explicit 6-value orbit K, K−s, −s, −K, s−K, s (s = secondCont ks) selected by j mod 6; on a nonempty large-quotient tail, continuant_replicate_one_append_pos_iff shows this is positive exactly for j ≡ 0, 1, 5 (mod 6) and continuant_replicate_one_append_ne_zero shows it never vanishes — the full mixed leading-1/large-quotient sign classification.

title: Trailing 1s — the period-6 law transfers to suffixes via reversal
content: Uses the §16 reversal bridge continuant_reverse to get the leading-1 orbit of §23 for free on the trailing end: continuant_append_replicate_one_eq shows appending j trailing 1s to ks equals prepending j leading 1s to ks.reverse, since (ks ++ 1ʲ).reverse = 1ʲ ++ ks.reverse. continuant_append_replicate_one_orbit transports the full §23 orbit, and continuant_append_replicate_one_pos_iff shows the sign law holds with the identical residues j ≡ 0, 1, 5 (mod 6) — because ks.reverse is again nonempty and all-≥2. continuant_append_replicate_one_ne_zero mirrors the non-vanishing result.
mathContext: $(ks{+}\!+1^j).\mathrm{reverse} = 1^j{+}\!+ks.\mathrm{reverse}$, so the trailing law equals the leading law on the reverse.

title: Interior 1-runs — the period-6 law at a Stern–Brocot junction, unconditionally
content: Handles the configuration a density count would actually sum over: a 1-run wedged between two arbitrary blocks, as ++ 1ʲ ++ bs. Peeling the leading block with Euler's composition law (continuant_append, §16) and substituting the §23 joint period-6 pair for the trailing part, continuant_interior_replicate_one_period proves K(as ++ 1^{j+6} ++ bs) = K(as ++ 1ʲ ++ bs) for EVERY pair of blocks — no large-quotient hypothesis at all. continuant_interior_replicate_one_half gives the half-turn K(as ++ 1^{j+3} ++ bs) = −K(as ++ 1ʲ ++ bs), and the headline continuant_interior_replicate_one_orbit collapses the whole orbit to three magnitudes v₀, v₁, v₂ (the direct junction and one/two inserted 1s) and their negations, selected by j mod 6.
mathContext: $K(as{+}\!+1^j{+}\!+bs)$ is period-6 in $j$ for ALL blocks $as,bs$, unconditionally.

title: Quotient-weighted growth — large quotients force short runs (toward O(n/d))
content: Sharpens §17's slope-1 bound to a quotient-floor-sensitive one. On a list with every entry ≥ d (d ≥ 2), continuant_ge_length_weighted proves the continuant grows with slope d−1: (d−1)·|ks| + 1 ≤ Continuant ks, re-running the §17 induction with the floor d carried through. continuant_run_length_le reads off the corollary: any continuant ceiling N forces |ks| ≤ (N−1)/(d−1), the first genuinely d-sensitive run-length cap, O(n/d) once paired with the order-n Farey ceiling N = n. continuant_ge_length_eq_weighted_two confirms d=2 recovers exactly §17's continuant_ge_length.

title: The interior 1-blow-down — a single interior 1 decrements its neighbours
content: A single interior 1 is not a fresh degree of freedom but a neighbour-decrementing contraction. stepMat_one_blowdown is the pure matrix identity M(a)·M(1)·M(b) = M(a−1)·M(b−1); reading its top-left entry through Euler's composition law gives the unconditional headline continuant_interior_one_blowdown: K(xs ++ [a,1,b] ++ ys) = K(xs ++ [a−1,b−1] ++ ys), for any surrounding blocks. continuant_two_one_two exhibits the elementary zero K[2,1,2] = 0 as the a=b=2 instance, and continuant_interior_one_eq_blowdown identifies §25's v₁ orbit magnitude precisely as such a blowdown — connecting the two sections' language.

title: Two-sided product bounds — the multiplicative refinement of §26
content: Sharpens §26's additive slope bound to a multiplicative sandwich. On the large-quotient regime, continuant_le_prod proves the upper bound Continuant ks ≤ ks.prod (dropping the nonnegative secondCont term at each step), and prod_sub_one_le_continuant proves the lower bound (ks.map (·−1)).prod ≤ Continuant ks (replacing secondCont by its ceiling K(rest)−1). continuant_prod_bounds packages both as the headline sandwich ∏(kᵢ−1) ≤ K(ks) ≤ ∏kᵢ, verified concretely on [3,3]: 4 ≤ K[3,3]=8 ≤ 9. The lower product is the genuinely geometric statement — on an all-≥d run it is ≥ (d−1)^|ks|, feeding the logarithmic cap of §30.

title: The equality locus of the product ceiling — strictness beyond length 1
content: Pins down exactly when §28's upper bound Continuant ks ≤ ks.prod is tight. continuant_prod_deficit shows a quantitative deficit at each head step: the product overshoots the continuant by at least the trailing continuant of the tail, secondCont(rest) ≤ (k::rest).prod − Continuant(k::rest). Since that trailing continuant is ≥ 1 once the tail is nonempty (§17 continuant_pos), continuant_lt_prod concludes the product ceiling is strict as soon as |ks| ≥ 2, and continuant_eq_prod_iff characterises equality exactly at the two trivial depths |ks| ≤ 1. Verified concretely: K[3,3] = 8 < 9 = 3·3, with deficit 1 matching secondCont[3] = 1.

title: Geometric growth and the logarithmic run-length cap
content: Formalises the consequence §28's product floor only advertised informally. pow_sub_one_le_prod_sub_one shows each decremented factor kᵢ−1 ≥ d−1, so (d−1)^|ks| ≤ ∏(kᵢ−1); chaining this through §28's prod_sub_one_le_continuant gives the headline geometric floor continuant_ge_pow: (d−1)^|ks| ≤ Continuant ks on an all-≥d run. The corollary continuant_run_length_le_log then caps the run length logarithmically — |ks| ≤ Nat.log(d−1) N under any continuant ceiling N, for d ≥ 3 — an exponential sharpening of §26's O(N/d) additive cap. Concretely, [3,3,3] has continuant 21 ≥ 2³ = 8, giving a length cap of Nat.log 2 21 = 4.

title: The geometric ceiling and the two-sided logarithmic sandwich
content: Supplies the matching upper direction to §30's floor. prod_le_pow shows that if every quotient is also bounded above by D, the product satisfies ks.prod ≤ D^|ks|, so continuant_le_pow gives Continuant ks ≤ D^|ks| — a geometric ceiling. continuant_run_length_ge_log then reads off a lower bound on the run length: a continuant floor N forces log_D N ≤ |ks|. The headline continuant_run_length_log_sandwich combines both directions for a bounded-quotient run (every entry in [d,D], d ≥ 3): log_D(K) ≤ |ks| ≤ log_{d−1}(K), pinning the run length to Θ(log K) — equivalently Θ(log n) under the order-n Farey cap. Concretely, [3,3,3] (continuant 21) satisfies log₃21=2 ≤ 3 ≤ 4=log₂21.
mathContext: $\log_D K(ks) \le |ks| \le \log_{d-1} K(ks)$ for a bounded-quotient run $d\le k_i\le D$.

title: Strict growth from the right end — the append dual of §17 monotonicity
content: Uses the §16 reversal bridge to get, for free, the trailing-end counterpart of §17's continuant_strict_mono. continuant_append_strict_mono shows appending a quotient k ≥ 2 on the right strictly increases the continuant, K(ks) < K(ks ++ [k]), by rewriting K(ks ++ [k]) = K(k :: ks.reverse) via continuant_reverse and applying the prepend monotonicity to the reversed (still all-≥2) list. The headline continuant_lt_cons_append chains both directions: bracketing a run ks by quotients ≥ 2 on both ends strictly increases the continuant past the inner run's value — the metric statement that a large-quotient run grows strictly when extended at either end, verified concretely by K[3]=3 < K[2,3,2]=13.
